item.research_question: How can supervised learning strategies combining canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and genetic algorithms (GA) be used to efficiently screen the vast compositional space of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to identify candidates with high hardness and reasonable ductility?
item.material_system: Multi-principal element alloys and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 5 or more elements; specifically, a 16-element palette (Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al, Cu, Mn, Ti, Mo, Nb, Ta, V, W, Zr, Zn, Sn) and synthesized candidates including Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03 and Ti18Ni24Ta12Cr22Co24.
item.processing_route: Synthesis of candidate alloys via arc-melting compressed pellets of elemental, high-purity powders (Sigma-Aldrich, purity ≥99.9%); pellets were remelted four times to ensure homogeneity; resulting as-cast solid pieces were polished for micro-hardness testing.
item.test_conditions: Vicker's indentation hardness testing using a LECO LM 248AT model hardness tester with a 100 g load applied for 10 s; at least 20 indents conducted per alloy; ductility assessed via optical microscopic inspection of indentations for cracks.
key_findings: A multiple regression analysis of 82 HE alloys yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.79 ± 0.07 between alloy metrics and normalized hardness.
Canonical correlation analysis identified three predictor variables especially relevant to hardness: ΔS′mix (positively correlated), ΔH′mix (negatively correlated), and VEC′ (negatively correlated).
A genetic algorithm (GA) with 1000 generations successfully evolved a population of alloys with fitness values 10–15% greater than the maximum found in the original dataset.
Seven candidate alloys synthesized by arc-melting were tested; five of the seven measured hardnesses fell within the 90% prediction interval of the model.
The highest measured hardness was 1084 ± 37 HV for Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03.
The second highest measured hardness was 1011 ± 20 HV for Ti18Ni24Ta12Cr22Co24.
All seven synthesized alloys exhibited Pugh ductility ratios (P) less than 0.5, with some showing moderate to considerable ductility (>50% of indentations without cracks).

Microstructural analysis of the hardest alloy (Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03) revealed a dendritic structure with 13 vol.% inter-dendritic phase, where the hardness was attributed to significant volume fraction of Nb–W solid solution strengthening.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that compositional disorder (high ΔS′mix) enhances hardness, while phase separation (high ΔH′mix) and high valence electron concentration (high VEC′) are associated with lower hardness. The high hardness of specific alloys is attributed to solid solution strengthening from significant volume fractions of Nb–W phases, whereas lower hardness in others may result from non-uniform element distribution or the presence of Ta.
item.limitations: The authors note that the Pugh criterion is an empirical proxy for ductility and serves as a rough predictor; they also state that further microstructural and computational analysis is needed to confirm the statistical insights regarding the physics of hardness; additionally, the hardest alloy showed some brittleness with cracking near indentation corners.
item.future_work: The authors propose using the methodology to investigate the impact of processing on property measurements (e.g., mechanical alloying vs. arc-melting), applying the CCA and GA to other properties like yield strength or corrosion resistance, and performing multi-objective Pareto optimization to simultaneously maximize hardness and ductility.
quotes: We describe here a supervised learning strategy for the efficient screening of HE alloys that combines two complementary tools, namely: (1) a multiple regression analysis and its generalization, a canonical-correlation analysis (CCA) and (2) a genetic algorithm (GA) with a CCA-inspired fitness function.

The highest measured hardnesses were found for Co33 W07 Al33 Nb24 Cr03 (1084 ± 37 HV) and Ti18 Ni24 Ta12 Cr22 Co24 (1011 ± 20 HV) that have corresponding Pugh ductility ratios of P = 0.38 and P = 0.47, respectively.
One possible explanation is that the high hardness of Co33 W07 Al33 Nb24 Cr03 is attributable to the significant volume fraction of the Nb–W phase, which is solid solution strengthened.
